issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: For chronic physical abuse by a romantic partner, being triggered by male presence and related people is coherent, but explosion/bang sounds points toward combat, accidents, or blast-related trauma and is hard to reconcile as a core trigger here without any matching assault-context cue elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: The rest of the profile reflects fear, avoidance, hypervigilance, fragmented memory, and negative self/world appraisals. Endorsing risky behavior pulls in the opposite direction and is not supported by other selected items; it reads as a different coping/symptom pattern than the otherwise strongly avoidant-threat profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: A marked loss of connection to community and culture is not well anchored to the rest of this intimate-partner-violence profile. The other appraisals center on danger, contamination, and shattered beliefs, but nothing else suggests cultural/community rupture, making this item feel clinically disconnected rather than tightly linked to the stated trauma formulation.

vignette:
Marianne was an 80-year-old European American woman who had spent much of her adult life working as a social worker, a role that had long required her to sit with other people’s pain in a calm, steady way. By the time she came for help, however, she described her own life as having become “smaller and more guarded” than she ever expected. In her early adulthood she had been in a relationship with a man she initially trusted, and over time that relationship became physically abusive. She did not tell the story as a single continuous narrative so much as in separate, sharp pieces. When she tried to recall what had happened, she would pause and say that the memories would not line up in the right order. What came back were a few moments only: a door opening too hard, a man standing too close, the sudden bodily sense of being trapped. Each fragment returned as if it were an image rather than a story, vivid and complete in itself, but disconnected from the next. When she spoke about those moments, she often became tearful and said that what she felt most, even now, was an overwhelming grief, not only for what had happened to her but for the person she had been before it.

The abuse left Marianne with a set of reactions that continued to shape her ordinary routines decades later. She became intensely uneasy around men, especially if she was alone with them, and she made careful use of distance whenever possible. Even in adulthood, and despite having worked professionally with a wide range of people, she remained wary of being in a room or building where she had to rely on a man she did not know well. She also found that related people, particularly men connected to someone she knew, could set off the same immediate alarm. A nephew arriving unexpectedly, a brother-in-law stepping into a kitchen, or a male colleague lingering after a meeting could leave her tense and preoccupied, watching them closely and waiting for something to change. Certain sounds pulled her back as well, especially doors opening or slamming. In her apartment and at her office, the sound of a heavy door hitting a frame could make her body react before she had fully registered what she heard. She would go still, listen, and then look toward the nearest exit.

That habit of checking exits became one of the most visible ways her life had narrowed. As soon as she entered any room or building, she scanned for doors, windows, and paths out. In restaurants, medical offices, and community spaces, her eyes moved automatically toward the nearest way to leave. She described herself as superalert and watchful, as though some part of her were always on duty. This vigilance followed her into sleep as well. She had trouble falling asleep and often woke during the night, then lay awake listening to sounds in the building and thinking about whether anything was wrong. Her evenings became especially difficult because she learned to avoid the times of day and situations that tended to bring on nightmares. If she noticed fatigue deepening into the late evening, she would sometimes stay up reading or switching on a light rather than letting herself drift off, because she had come to expect that certain hours carried a greater risk of disturbing dreams.

Marianne also tried to manage the memories themselves in ways that gave her some sense of control. At times she made a deliberate effort to erase the event from her mind, pushing away images as soon as they surfaced and telling herself not to dwell on them. Yet she also found herself doing the opposite, thinking repeatedly about why the event had happened to her. She would ask, with a kind of exhausted disbelief, what it meant that she had been the one chosen for that treatment, and why someone who said he cared could have acted that way. These thoughts were not comforting to her; they were part of the way she struggled to make sense of a past that felt morally and emotionally impossible to her. She said her beliefs about how the world works had been completely destroyed. Where she once assumed that ordinary relationships could be trusted and that people generally meant what they said, she now felt that people could not be trusted. That mistrust extended beyond romance into everyday interactions, though she did not describe herself as isolated so much as cautious to the point of strain.

Another feeling she described with distress was a sense of being dirty or contaminated because of what had happened. She did not mean this in a literal sense, but as an enduring stain on her sense of self. Even after all these years, the assaultive relationship left her feeling marked in a way she could not wash off. Speaking about it brought that feeling to the surface, along with the grief and the effort of holding her composure. By the time she sought treatment, Marianne said she was tired of arranging her life around fear, tired of losing sleep, and tired of the sudden jolt she felt whenever a door slammed or she found herself alone with a man. What brought her in at last was the sense that these reactions had become too costly to keep carrying alone. More than anything, she hoped to sleep without dread and to feel, at least sometimes, that the world and the people in it might still be safe enough to live in.
